$comment: Generated by node contract/tools/generate.mjs. Edit contract/tools, not these files.
notes: merges: baseText is the base the device chose (bases gives the rule), or null when there is none. mineHash and theirsHash are the canonical hashes of mineText and theirsText. choices maps an entry key to mine or theirs; an entry it does not name takes mine when its kind is mine and theirs otherwise.

merges: theirsText and baseText pass section 9.7 under peer intake. mineText is the applied document, kept by applied intake, and may break unknown-site, helper-self, helper-unknown, helper-alias and helper-cycle; it is merged all the same. A mine with any other error, and a theirs or base that peer intake refuses, is not merged at all: a client checks that before it offers Merge or Keep mine, and no case starts such a merge.

merges: differences lists every entry where mine and theirs differ, in code-point order of the key, with its kind: mine or theirs (with a base, the side that changed it), both (with a base, both changed it, a deletion against an edit included) or noBase.

merges: resultText is the merged document, or null when section 9.7 refuses it under peer intake; error is then the first of its error codes in code-point order. Compare resultText as a parsed document: object key order ignored, array order exact, number lexemes exact.

Entry keys: <key> for a top-level key other than controller, machines and sites, written "<key>" (inside double quotes, nothing escaped) when it begins with ", controller., sites[ or machines[; controller.<key> for a controller key other than id, revision, updatedAt, source, device and lineage; sites[<id>]; machines[<id>] when only one side has the machine; machines[<id>].fields, .wake, .systems[<id>], .endpoints[<id>] and .endpoints[] (the endpoints without an id, in order, as one value) when both have it.
bases: kept maps a hash to the text this device kept for it. The base is the first hash of mineLineage that is in theirsLineage, whose kept text hashes to it and which peer intake accepts, or null.
numbers: a and b are JSON number lexemes, equal when they are the same decimal value.

merges.name: both-sides-applied
merges.purpose: Theirs renames pi and mine adds an endpoint to tower. Each side changed a different entry, so each is taken from the side that changed it and nobody is asked.

merges.name: delete-versus-edit-keep-deletion
merges.purpose: Mine deletes tower while theirs edits its lan endpoint. Delete against edit is one question about the whole machine, never a silent winner; answered mine, tower is gone.

merges.name: delete-versus-edit-take-edit
merges.purpose: The same question left at its default, theirs: the edited tower comes back, at the position it has in theirs, which is first.

merges.name: theirs-deletes-what-mine-edited
merges.purpose: Theirs deletes tower while mine edits its wake block. The question is shown, and its default, theirs, removes the machine.

merges.name: mine-deletes-unchanged-machine
merges.purpose: Mine deletes a tower theirs left as the base had it, so the deletion is mine alone and is kept; theirs' rename of nas is taken.

merges.name: delete-versus-edit-endpoint
merges.purpose: Mine deletes the remote endpoint of tower, theirs changes its host. One endpoint, both changed it: asked, and theirs by default.

merges.name: theirs-adds-idless-endpoint
merges.purpose: Theirs adds an endpoint without an id between lan and remote. It is kept, Android dropped it, and lands after its predecessor in theirs.

merges.name: both-change-idless-endpoints
merges.purpose: Both sides change the endpoint without an id. The endpoints without an id are one entry, so this is one question; theirs by default replaces mine's.

merges.name: idless-endpoints-keep-their-place
merges.purpose: nas has two endpoints without an id and theirs adds wifi after them. Theirs' n-th endpoint without an id stands for the result's n-th, so the cursor passes both and wifi lands last, where theirs has it, not first and not after the first one.

merges.name: endpoint-between-idless-endpoints
merges.purpose: nas has three endpoints without an id and theirs adds wifi between the second and the third. Each of theirs' endpoints without an id moves the cursor to its counterpart in the result, in order, so wifi lands between the same two there.

merges.name: unknown-top-level-keys
merges.purpose: Theirs edits the unknown top-level notes, and both add an unknown extra with different values. Unknown keys are entries like any other: notes from theirs, extra asked.

merges.name: controller-keys
merges.purpose: Theirs renames the setup and changes an unknown controller key, mine renames nas. Both controller keys are entries taken from theirs; the identity is the merge's own.

merges.name: insert-after-predecessor
merges.purpose: Endpoints lan, wifi, remote. Theirs edits wifi and adds vpn after lan; mine renames tower. The result is lan, vpn, wifi as theirs has it, remote: replaced in place, inserted after its predecessor, never moved to the end.

merges.name: reorder-only
merges.purpose: Theirs only reorders tower's endpoints. A reorder alone is not a difference: nothing is asked, and mine's order stays.

merges.name: number-spelling
merges.purpose: nas carries "weight": 22.0 on every side and is untouched; mine writes the unknown threshold as 1e2 where theirs keeps 100. Equal numbers are no difference, and nothing not replaced is printed differently: 22.0 and 1e2 stay as written.

merges.name: no-base
merges.purpose: No kept revision is a common ancestor. Nothing says who changed what, so every difference is noBase, shown, and theirs by default: mine's rename of tower is undone unless the person keeps it.

merges.name: long-lineages
merges.purpose: Mine is revision 40 and theirs 39, each with a lineage of 20. The merge is revision 41, and its lineage is both heads, then the two lineages interleaved mine first, cut at 32.

merges.name: keep-mine
merges.purpose: Keep mine is a merge with every entry answered mine, including the ones theirs alone changed: mine's content, under a new revision whose lineage holds theirs' head, so theirs fast-forwards onto it.

merges.name: choice-breaks-a-rule
merges.purpose: Theirs makes pi a helper of tower and renames it; mine deletes pi, and the person keeps the deletion. The result would name a helper that does not exist, so nothing is written and the rule is named.

merges.name: theirs-adds-site
merges.purpose: Theirs adds a site and moves nas to it. The new site is inserted after its predecessor and the machine's own fields are taken with its new site.

merges.name: both-add-machines
merges.purpose: Theirs adds laptop after tower, mine adds studio at the end. Each lands where its side put it.

merges.name: theirs-deletes-endpoint
merges.purpose: Theirs deletes an endpoint mine left alone, mine renames pi: the deletion is taken.

merges.name: both-edit-system-keep-mine
merges.purpose: Both rename tower's system; the person keeps mine.

merges.name: theirs-removes-unknown-key
merges.purpose: Theirs removes the unknown top-level notes mine left alone: removed in the result too.

merges.name: wake-and-fields-separately
merges.purpose: Mine changes tower's wake ports, theirs renames tower. A machine both sides have merges part by part, so both edits are kept.

merges.name: theirs-adds-first-system
merges.purpose: nas has no systems key; theirs gives it one. The array mine never had is created, appended to the machine, for the system that goes in it.

merges.name: mine-with-error-repaired
merges.purpose: Mine breaks section 9.7: an edit outside the app deleted pi and left tower's helper naming it (helper-unknown). Applied intake keeps that document, so it is still merged. Theirs renamed pi, the question is left at theirs, pi comes back, and the result passes.

merges.name: mine-with-error-kept
merges.purpose: The same mine with the question answered mine, which is Keep mine: the result still names a helper that does not exist, so nothing is written and the rule mine already broke is named.

merges.name: top-level-keys-like-entries
merges.purpose: Unknown top-level keys named sites[home] and controller.name. Their keys are written in quotes, so theirs' edit of the member "sites[home]" and mine's rename of the site home are two entries, and so are mine's edit of the member "controller.name" and theirs' rename of the setup.

bases.name: newest-common-ancestor
bases.purpose: The first hash of mine's lineage that is also in theirs' and whose kept bytes hash to it.

bases.name: newest-common-not-kept
bases.purpose: The newest common ancestor is no longer kept here, so the next one is the base.

bases.name: kept-bytes-changed
bases.purpose: The bytes kept under the newest common hash no longer hash to it, so they are not that revision and the next common one is the base.

bases.name: kept-revision-refused
bases.purpose: The revision kept under the newest common hash is one peer intake refuses, kept by an older build, so it is skipped like one that is not kept and the next common one is the base.

bases.name: only-common-revision-refused
bases.purpose: The only revision both sides descend from is one peer intake refuses: there is no base, and every difference is asked about.

bases.name: no-common-ancestor
bases.purpose: Nothing in common: there is no base, and every difference is noBase.

bases.name: head-is-not-a-base
bases.purpose: Theirs descends from mine's head and mine's bytes are kept, but a head is never a base: the base is the newest common ancestor of the two lineages.

numbers.name: integer-and-decimal
numbers.purpose: 22 and 22.0 are one number: the Mac printed the second as the first.

numbers.name: close-decimals
numbers.purpose: 0.1 and 0.10000000000000001 are two numbers, though a double cannot tell them apart.

numbers.name: large-integers
numbers.purpose: 9007199254740993 and 9007199254740992 are two numbers, though a double rounds the first to the second.

numbers.name: large-integer-and-exponent
numbers.purpose: A 30-digit integer and the same value written with an exponent are one number.
